Disease Outbreak Disrupts Uzbekistan’s Engineering & Construction Workforce

TASHKENT – An outbreak of gastrointestinal illness has struck multiple engineering and construction sites across Uzbekistan, severely impacting project timelines and workforce availability in the sector. The Ministry of Health confirmed on Thursday that at least 230 workers have been hospitalized since last weekend, with hundreds more reportedly affected by symptoms including fever, abdominal pain, and diarrhea.

China Petroleum Engineering Corp is among the companies reporting significant staff shortages due to the outbreak at its major pipeline project in the Karakalpakstan region. “We are cooperating closely with local health authorities to contain the situation and safeguard our workers’ health,” said a spokesperson for China Petroleum Engineering Corp. “Several key activities have been paused pending further medical clearance.”

The illness appears to have spread rapidly through temporary worker accommodation sites, according to the Uzbekistan Construction Union. “Among the hardest hit are teams involved in infrastructure and energy projects,” said union representative Nodira Yuldasheva. “At some sites, up to 40% of the workforce is currently absent. This is placing immense pressure on companies to meet deadlines and maintain safety standards.”

Local health officials believe contaminated water supplies at several large-scale construction camps may be the source of the outbreak. Investigations are ongoing, and water quality testing has been intensified. “We urge all companies to ensure strict hygiene protocols and provide bottled water until the situation is under control,” said Dr. Akmal Tursunov, head of the Ministry’s outbreak response team.

The disruptions have already led to delays in project delivery dates, with some contractors warning of potential contractual penalties. Kamoliddin Construction, which is managing a residential complex in Tashkent, reported that excavation and foundation works have been put on hold for at least a week. “We are prioritizing our workers’ health, but this comes at a significant operational cost,” said site manager Shavkat Rasulov.

Analysts caution that continued absenteeism and site closures could have ripple effects on the sector’s productivity for weeks to come. “Engineering and construction projects operate on tight schedules and margins,” said industry consultant Dilshod Karimov. “Even a short-term disruption can result in cascading delays and increased costs.”

As of Thursday evening, medical teams remained stationed at several affected sites, and further updates from health authorities and companies are expected in the coming days.
